extracted.intended_audience: artists, architects, craftsmen, art-historians, and patrons interested in Renaissance art and architecture
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative observations on the quality of stained-glass painting, fresco/panel painting, ironwork, masonry, and architectural design in the Renaissance (illustrated with examples of masters and anti-patterns). Useful for judging craft, proportion, and durability in built and decorative works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition and grouping of scenes (stained glass)
rubrics_metrics.description: "composition of scenes, making them rich and well grouped"; designing pictures with such good method and order that mountings are fitted into joinings and folds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mountings of lead and iron should be so fitted into the joinings of the figures and the folds of the draperies that they cannot be seen and even give the whole such grace. Good composition makes a stained-glass window read as a coherent picture rather than a collection of pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of structural mountings into design
rubrics_metrics.description: Design windows so that the mountings (lead and iron) are incorporated into the design rather than visible interruptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fit the lead/iron mountings into joinings and folds of figures so they are not visible; this can 'make a virtue of necessity' by turning unavoidable structural elements into compositional features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shading colours for fired glass (iron and copper scales)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of two kinds of colour for shading when subjecting glass to fire: 'one was scale of iron, and the other scale of copper.' Iron (dark) for draperies, hair, buildings; copper (tawny) for flesh tones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply iron-based pigments for dark shading and copper-based for warm/flesh tints. Also employ hematite (pounded and ground, tempered with gum) for burnishing gold; these material choices affect final tonality and durability after firing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flashing technique and multi-layer colour effects
rubrics_metrics.description: "the glasses are flashed; that is, in some places the first skin has been removed, and the glass then coloured with another tint" (e.g., placing yellow over red flashed glass, or white/green over blue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flashing (removing the thin coloured skin and re-colouring) allows intricate colour layering. It is difficult and requires skill (use of pointed iron or grinding with a copper wheel and emery). Skilled flashing produces subtle, multi-layered colour effects not achievable by simple surface painting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firing for durability over mere transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Firing in the furnace and making glass such that it will withstand the action of water and remain fresh for ever is the difficult and praiseworthy part of the craft; painting with oil or making it diaphanous is of less importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize methods that penetrate and fuse colour into glass (e.g., calcined silver painted before firing) so the colour takes a firm hold and endures. Durable firing is essential to long-lived stained-glass work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical methods for safe surface reduction (anti-cracking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many, fearing breakage, avoid using a pointed iron to remove flashed layers and instead grind the glass with a copper wheel and emery to leave only a thin layer of white glass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When skill or risk of breakage is an issue, use grinding with progressively finer abrasives to remove flashed layers safely. This technique trades time for reduced breakage risk while achieving clarity for subsequent colouring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of calcined silver (bole-like) for yellow on flashed glass
rubrics_metrics.description: When a yellow colour must be applied to flashed-and-ground glass, at the moment it is placed in the furnace it is painted with calcined silver (a bole-like thick colour) which melts and penetrates the glass during firing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply calcined metal-based pigments immediately before firing so they fuse into the glass and produce stable yellows and other tones that will not flake or wash away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawing skill as foundational to improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Although not initially a great draughtsman, the artist 'applied himself to the study of drawing' and 'little by little he achieved the improvement' evident in later windows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate drawing ability regardless of age; improved draughtsmanship materially elevates the design and execution of painted or glass imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Density of composition and naturalism in small spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to include many figures, show terror, amazement, stench, etc., and render landscapes, temples in perspective and staircases so natural 'that one would never think it was glass'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for convincing narrative detail and naturalistic rendering even within small panels: expressive figures, perspective architecture, and realistic landscapes make glass read like painting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Layering of colours 'one over the other' for richness
rubrics_metrics.description: Works contain 'innumerable colours, flashed one over the other in the glass', yielding natural and convincing detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple flashed and fused colour layers to build chromatic richness; this is a sign of advanced technical mastery in glasswork.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation of antique models with judgment, proportion, and fitness
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not enough to copy ancient models with exact measurements; the difficulty lies in 'accommodating them to the purpose which they have to serve, with grace, true measurement, proportion, and fitness.' Example: Cronaca copied an antique cornice but enlarged it suitably; Baccio d'Agnolo copied a large cornice onto a small façade and produced ugliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drawing on ancient forms, adapt proportions and scale to the new context. Good judgment and the eye matter more than literal measurement—poor adaptation leads to disproportion and visual failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good judgment and the eye over slavish measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Good judgment and the eye play a greater part in all such matters than measuring with compasses.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train aesthetic judgment and proportion-sense rather than relying solely on exact copies; evaluate how a borrowed element reads on the entire façade or structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stone masonry balance and finish (counterpoising stones)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stones were 'counterpoising the stones in such a way, in order that they might turn out well bound and balanced, that there is no better masonry to be seen... all the other stones are so well put together ... that the whole does not appear to be of masonry, but rather all of one piece.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure stones are balanced and well-bonded; counterpoise courses to achieve an integrated, monolithic appearance and high finish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excellence in ironwork design and execution
rubrics_metrics.description: Iron lanterns and iron ornaments executed with 'supreme diligence' showing cornices, columns, capitals, and brackets of iron fixed together with wonderful craftsmanship; 'no modern ever executed in iron works so large and so difficult, and with such knowledge and mastery.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ironwork should be conceived as integral decorative architecture — well-drawn, proportioned, and executed with structural and ornamental mastery. The quality of finish and inventiveness of iron pieces significantly contribute to overall architectural distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roof-truss and large structural design (practical engineering detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: For large roofs, make tie-beams of many timbers well scarfed and fastened together when single beams are unavailable; use king-posts and queen-posts (three per truss), long rafters, struts properly thrusting against rafters and each other; place tie-beams at intervals (example: six braccia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural carpentry must be designed to span large proportions safely: scarfing, multiple posts, well-arranged struts, and appropriate spacing are essential. Detailed attention to these elements allows construction when single large timbers are not obtainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ceiling compartmentalization and ornament proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: Ceiling formed of plain wood divided into panels 'each of which was four braccia square and surrounded by an ornamental cornice of few members'; flat moulding encloses panels with large bosses at intersections and corners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design ceiling compartments with consistent panel proportions and harmonious mouldings. Panel size, framing, and decorative bosses should relate to the room scale to avoid visual awkwardness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hall proportions, lighting, and relation to scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Large halls must avoid being 'too dark, and also stunted and wanting in height in relation to its great length and breadth; in short, almost wholly out of proportion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure adequate height and windowing for large halls so that length and breadth do not overbear vertical scale. Adjust walls and add windows or raise the roof if necessary to maintain balanced proportions and light.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staircase slope and user convenience
rubrics_metrics.description: A great staircase may be richly adorned, but if it is 'inconvenient and too steep' it loses practical merit; a gently rising staircase is preferred (example: later Vasari staircase almost like walking on the level).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design staircases for comfortable ascent (gentle pitch) within available space; ornament should not compromise usability. Compare alternative layouts to achieve both grandeur and convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonizing interiors to pre-existing exteriors when constrained
rubrics_metrics.description: When forced to adapt interiors to an outer shell begun by others, the architect should 'attend to giving it such beauty as it displays' and is to be excused some discrepancies, but must strive for harmony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When working within pre-existing constraints, seek solutions that reconcile interior function and proportion with the exterior shell, aiming to preserve overall beauty despite limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic invention, abundance of figures, and grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Mastery is shown in 'composition, or invention, or colouring, or general excellence' and in being 'born for that profession' producing works with 'beauty, in abundance of figures, or in grace.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess paintings and windows for originality of invention, compositional variety, graceful figure handling, and overall beauty — these qualities distinguish exceptional masters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Site selection, measurement, and classical learning for architects
rubrics_metrics.description: Good architects show 'good judgment in choosing sites' and imitate antiquity by 'having observed the rules of Vitruvius and the works of Filippo di Ser Brunellesco.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Architectural excellence requires careful site selection, measured study of antique precedents, and application of classical principles (proportion, orders) adapted to present needs.
